claims.text: The alloy begins as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution with a uniform elemental distribution.
Service-like mechanical loading induces nanoscale phase separation or compositional segregation in the initially homogeneous alloy.
The mechanically induced segregated regions form brittle interphase boundaries.
Cu-rich grain boundaries significantly reduce ductility in the Co-Cr-Cu-Fe-Ni high-entropy alloy.
Phase separation creates regions with different mechanical properties and critical resolved shear stresses.
Phase separation produces an uneven local stress distribution.
Segregated regions impede smooth dislocation motion.
Segregation-induced mechanical mismatch causes localized plastic instability.
The segregated regions promote early microcrack nucleation and crack propagation.
Loading-induced segregation reduces fracture toughness and fracture energy relative to the homogeneous baseline.
Fracture surfaces will exhibit intergranular or interphase brittle features spatially associated with segregated regions.
Elevated temperature, high strain rate, or prolonged cyclic loading can provide sufficient local stress concentration to initiate phase separation.
Below critical service-loading thresholds, the alloy may retain its initial toughness.
Suppressing phase separation should mitigate the loss of toughness or brittle fracture.
Rapid cooling or alloying modifications can serve as stabilization treatments that suppress segregation.
Toughness loss without detectable segregation, or failure of segregation suppression to mitigate embrittlement, would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The comparator is described both as an as-cast homogeneous baseline and as being tested under identical loading conditions. Under the hypothesis, identical service loading could itself induce segregation, so the baseline cannot be assumed to remain as-cast and homogeneous without an explicit stabilization or pre-loading comparison.

The two sets are said to have identical initial microstructures, but the proposed control may use alloying modifications. Changing alloy composition would not constitute an otherwise identical sample and could independently alter toughness and fracture behavior.
